title: 8. Stage 2 Technical Structure, Institutional Flow & Momentum Setup

epigraph.quote: A great company in a Stage 4 downtrend is still a falling knife until institutions step back in above the 30-week moving average on expanding volume.
epigraph.author: Stan Weinstein Tape Discipline

web_blocks.html: General Dynamics cleared Pass 1 as a COMPOUNDER_PASS business, yet its chart says to keep cash on the sidelines. At the November 18, 2026 close of $348.26, GD sits in a Stan Weinstein Stage 4 posture (AVOID_STAGE4_OR_BROKEN, gate: CAP_REJECTED) [14]. Shares are down -12.94% from the $400.00 52-week high (low: $306.77) [14]. The stock also fell -10.01% over three months and -5.68% over the past week [14].

web_blocks.takeaway: GD sits below its $358.57 weekly shelf and 200-day SMA ($355.00), with 4H RSI at 33.81 showing no turn. Until price holds $329.18–$339.20 support or reclaims $358.57 on volume, there is no short-term momentum edge.

web_blocks.html: Institutional ownership remains high at 88.09%, with +0.23% institutional flow and 0.86% short float [13]. That confirms GD is not facing aggressive short-seller pressure [13]. Instead, the pullback reflects broad market distribution (8 S&P 500 distribution days) and profit-taking off $400.00. Two setups would turn this tape constructive. First, a pullback into the $329.18–$339.20 support zone near Pivot S1 ($334.19) with a 4H/Daily higher-low reversal. Second, a high-volume Stage 1-to-Stage 2 reclaim above the $358.57 30-week SMA.

For options traders, the deterministic scan flags IV_FAIR (29.4% ATM IV vs. 26.7% 20-day HV). It models a defined-risk 2027-02-19 $340/$430 Bull Call Debit Spread (92 DTE) at a $20.40 net debit. Max loss is $2,040 per contract, max profit is $6,960 above $430 (3.41:1 R:R), and breakeven is $360.40. Because the 4H chart has not turned up and GD sits in Stage 4, even spread buyers should wait for 4H/Daily stabilization.

With 20-day Bollinger Band width at 9.31% and 14-day ATR at $7.73 (~2.2% daily range), volatility remains orderly [14]. Watch for higher weekly lows above Pivot S1 ($334.19) and a flattening 10-week EMA ($354.53) before expecting a breakout past $358.57 [14].

Actionable Chart Triggers & Invalidations: Exiting Stage 4 requires either a 4H/Daily higher-low reversal inside $329.18–$339.20, or a weekly close above $358.57 and $360.91 on >=1.2x volume [14]. Losing Pivot S1 ($334.19) and $315.00 opens downside risk toward Pivot S2 ($295.80) [14].

Options Desk Discipline: The 2027-02-19 $340/$430 Bull Call Spread ($20.40 debit, 3.41:1 R:R) prices IV fairly at 29.4% vs. 26.7% HV20. Still, options buyers should wait for 4H/Daily stabilization so daily theta (-$3.34/day) does not erode capital during a Stage 4 drift [14]. Right now, GD sits below its 50-day SMA ($348.99), 200-day SMA ($355.00), and 30-week SMA ($358.57) [14]. Daily volume of 318,971 shares is just 0.26x the 30-day average, showing light-volume drift rather than capitulation [14]. Until buyers step in at support or above $358.57, patience protects capital [14].

book_paragraphs: Chapter 7 told us that General Dynamics is fundamentally sound and reasonably priced. Now let us look at the tape in Chapter 8, because price structure tells us *when*—and *whether*—the market agrees with our spreadsheet.

Right now, the chart is telling us to wait. At $348.26, GD is in a Stan Weinstein Stage 4 posture. It sits 2.88% below its 30-week simple moving average of $358.57, 1.90% below its 200-day moving average of $355.00, and just beneath its 50-day moving average of $348.99. Over the last three months, the stock has slipped 10.01% from its $400.00 52-week high, including a 5.68% drop over the past week alone.

Let us zoom in across three timeframes—weekly, daily, and 4-hour—to see if buyers are defending any level yet. On the weekly chart, RSI sits at 47.28: neutral-to-weak, with the 10-week EMA at $354.53 sloping down as overhead supply. On the daily chart, RSI is 42.13, and the 20-day SMA at $360.91 sits right above the 30-week SMA, creating a thick ceiling of resistance between $355 and $361. On the 4-hour chart, RSI has cooled to 33.81, and price remains well below the 4-hour 20-EMA at $357.07. That means the intraday turn has not happened yet.

Volume confirms the picture. Yesterday's volume of 318,971 shares was just 0.26 times the 30-day average of 1.23 million shares. We are not seeing panic liquidation, and short interest is tiny at 0.86% of the float with 88.09% institutional ownership. Instead, GD is drifting lower in a broad U.S. market Downtrend where only 43.6% of S&P 500 stocks are above their 50-day moving average and the index has logged 8 distribution days.

So what is the disciplined trader's playbook here? We never buy Stage 4 breakouts, and we never average blindly into an unconfirmed 4-hour slide. There are only two clean setups on this chart. Setup A is a patient limit bid in the $329.18 to $339.20 support zone—centered right around Pivot S1 at $334.19—once the 4-hour chart stops making lower lows. Setup B is a trend-following reclaim above the $358.57 30-week SMA on above-average volume, which would signal that institutions are rotating back into defense.

In the Web Research Dossier, you will also see our Options Desk overlay. Because GD's 29.4% implied volatility is fairly priced against 26.7% 20-day realized volatility, a 92-day $340/$430 Bull Call Debit Spread expiring February 19, 2027 costs $20.40 per share ($2,040 maximum risk per contract) for a $6,960 maximum profit above $430. Even there, discipline comes first: wait for the 4-hour tape to turn before risking a single dollar.

Let us also look at volatility and range behavior so you know what a healthy bottoming process actually looks like on GD's chart. With a 14-day Average True Range of $7.73—roughly 2.2% of the stock price—and a 20-day Bollinger Band width of 9.31%, GD is not experiencing chaotic gap-downs. It is undergoing an orderly institutional digestion after hitting $400.00.

In Stan Weinstein's framework, an orderly digestion turns into a buyable Stage 1 base when two things happen: first, the stock stops making lower lows near Pivot S1 ($334.19) and begins to coil sideways with shrinking daily ranges; second, the 10-week EMA ($354.53) flattens out and price punches back above the 30-week SMA ($358.57) on at least 1.2 times average daily volume. Until you see one of those two footprints—either a confirmed 4-hour reversal inside $329.18–$339.20 or a volume reclaim of $358.57—staying patient in cash is the highest-edge move.

Make sure those exact price levels are written on a sticky note above your monitor. Between $349 and $361 sits a heavy overhead ceiling of moving averages—the 50-day SMA at $348.99, the 200-day SMA at $355.00, the 30-week SMA at $358.57, and the 20-day SMA at $360.91. Below today's $348.26 close sits Pivot S1 at $334.19, anchoring our $329.18–$339.20 support buy zone, with Pivot S2 far lower at $295.80. Until price proves itself at support or punches cleanly through $358.57 on volume, patience protects your capital.

Even if you prefer defined-risk options over outright shares, the same tape discipline applies. Yes, a $340/$430 Bull Call Spread expiring in February 2027 caps your worst-case loss at $2,040 per contract with a $360.40 breakeven. Yet entering that spread while the 4-hour RSI sits at 33.81 and the S&P 500 is in a Downtrend simply hands time decay to the market maker. Wait for the 4-hour trend to turn up first.
Respecting both the weekly moving-average ceiling and the 4-hour momentum structure keeps you out of premature Stage 4 drawdowns and preserves your capital for high-probability inflection points.

And remember: in a broad market Downtrend with eight distribution days on the S&P 500, waiting for either the .18–.20 support zone or a high-volume .57 reclaim is not passive—it is active risk management.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Respecting Stage 4 is what separates patient capital from trapped capital. You can admire GD's $220.3 billion submarine backlog all day long, but if the 30-week SMA ($358.57) and 4-hour EMA ($357.07) are both overhead and the S&P 500 is in a Downtrend, waiting for $329–$339 support or a $358.57 reclaim costs you nothing and saves you from catching a falling knife.
